one_liner: RFC 4180 C++ CSV reader/writer with mmap, SIMD and speculative parallel parsing; beats fast-cpp-csv-parser and rapidcsv on large-file ETL.
what_it_does: Streams CSV/TSV files of any size (including larger than RAM) through CSVReader, an input-iterator over CSVRow objects whose fields are fetched by index or column name and converted lazily with get<T>, try_get, std::optional or std::chrono timestamps. It handles quoted commas, doubled quotes, embedded newlines, CR/LF/CRLF, BOMs, variable row lengths and dialect inference, and also ships CSVWriter, JSON row export and a keyed DataFrame for random access and edits. The interface is dynamic (runtime schema), so it is not a drop-in for fast-cpp-csv-parser's compile-time typed read_row or for rapidcsv's Document.
how_it_is_fast: File inputs are memory-mapped and parsed in 10 MB chunks by a background producer thread while the caller consumes rows; rows are lightweight views into shared chunk buffers and fields are only converted when asked. A SIMD skip loop (AVX2, SSE2 or NEON, chosen at compile time) jumps to the next delimiter, quote, LF or CR. Since 5.0.0, files of 50 MB or more are split across workers with speculative parallel parsing after Ge et al., 'Speculative Distributed CSV Data Parsing for Big Data Analytics' (SIGMOD 2019): each chunk guesses its quote state and a validator repairs row fragments when the guess is wrong.
when_to_use: Real-world CSV with quoted fields, embedded line breaks, ragged rows or unknown delimiters, where fast-cpp-csv-parser throws or needs a fixed column count.

Large file-backed inputs (above the 50 MB speculative threshold) on a multi-core machine: with 4 to 8 parser workers positional reads beat fast-cpp-csv-parser (5M rows clean 702.2 / 605.0 ms vs 915.1 ms on an i5-12400).
Runtime schemas: lookup by column name, per-field type checks and conversions, JSON export, without writing a struct per file.
Load-edit-save table workflows: the DataFrame plus CSVWriter path beat rapidcsv 1.56x on load and 2.2x on load+save at 500K rows with a single parser worker.
WebAssembly or embedded builds that need a CSV reader without threads (CSV_ENABLE_THREADS=0 keeps the same API).
when_not_to_use: Single-core or small-file raw reads: with one parser worker it is slower than fast-cpp-csv-parser (500K rows count 146.5 vs 81.8 ms, read 164.9 vs 82.8 ms; 5M rows single-worker positional read 1,442 vs 915.1 ms).

Many repeated passes over materialized rows: lazy CSVRow fields are re-parsed on every get<>, so the multi-pass-only step was 3.4x slower than fast-cpp's pre-converted structs (479.5 vs 141.6 ms at 5M rows); convert once into your own structs.
Maximum raw scan throughput: its SIMD only skips to the next special byte; C parsers built around SIMD and parallel scanning, such as zsv, report far higher count rates.
Builds with -fno-exceptions: the library requires C++ exceptions.
Memory-tight hosts: speculative mode reads chunk_size x worker_count windows (10 MB x 12 workers on a 12-thread CPU), and a vector of CSVRow keeps every referenced 10 MB chunk alive.

integration.form: single generated header (csv.hpp) or CMake static lib (target csv); also on the Bazel Central Registry
integration.dependencies: none external (bundles string-view-lite for pre-C++17 and its classify_scalar conversion code); Threads::Threads when CSV_ENABLE_THREADS is on
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 minimum, C++20 default in CMake (CMake 3.15+); exceptions required; std::optional API needs C++17 and as<T>() needs C++23 std::expected
integration.platforms: any C++11 platform with std::thread (or threads disabled); SIMD paths for x86 AVX2/SSE2 and ARM NEON (since 5.1.0), selected at compile time; mmap replaced by ifstream on Emscripten; CI covers g++, clang, MSVC and MinGW
integration.thread_safety: One CSVReader per consumer thread; it runs its own background parser thread and, for files of 50 MB or more, speculative worker threads. Parallel processing of rows is offered through chunk_parallel_apply and DataFrame helpers; concurrent use of one reader is not documented.

gotchas: Harness flaw: the README labels the materialization, ETL and rapidcsv comparisons as single-parser-worker or single-threaded, but bench_format() leaves speculative_parallel_threads at 0 (auto = std::thread::hardware_concurrency(), 12 on the i5-12400) and the 50 MB threshold, and the 5M-row inputs are 297 MB (clean) to 445 MB (multiline), so at 5M rows csv-parser ran speculative parallel parsing against fast-cpp's one parser thread and rapidcsv's single thread. Timings agree: 5M materialize 739.6 ms vs the explicitly single-worker read 1,442 ms in the same session, while at 500K rows (28.7 MB, below threshold) materialize 156.8 ms matches the single-worker read 154.5 ms. The single-worker gains are the 500K rows: about 1.4x materialize and 1.1x materialize+aggregation over fast-cpp-csv-parser.
By default rows with missing or extra columns are silently dropped (VariableColumnPolicy::IGNORE_ROW); set THROW or KEEP if data loss matters.

CSVReader::iterator is an input iterator over chunks that are freed as it advances: std algorithms that need forward iterators are undefined behaviour, get<string_view> is valid only while its CSVRow lives, and parse_unsafe() requires the source string to outlive the rows.

On MSVC x86 the csv target adds /arch:AVX2 as a PUBLIC compile option, so every consumer is built for AVX2 with no runtime dispatch and will not run on pre-AVX2 CPUs unless CSV_NO_SIMD is set; GCC/Clang only take the AVX2 path when you pass -mavx2/-march (or CSV_FORCE_AVX2), otherwise SSE2 on x86-64.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over fast-cpp-csv-parser when files may contain quoted line breaks or ragged rows, the schema is only known at runtime, or the file is large and several cores are free; keep fast-cpp-csv-parser for fixed-schema files on one core. Pick zsv when you need the highest raw scan rate from a C library, and DuckDB or Polars when the goal is SQL or dataframe analytics rather than embedding a C++ reader.
verified_claims_summary: The author's Google Benchmark suite (median real time, generated 8-column CSV, Windows 11, MSVC 19.50 C++20 Release with /arch:AVX2 on the csv-parser binaries, Core i5-12400) shows csv-parser materializing 500K rows 1.4x faster than fast-cpp-csv-parser and about 1.1x faster with aggregation, but 1.8-2.0x slower on raw count and read; the larger 5M-row leads (2.8x materialize, 1.8-2.0x ETL, 3.45-4.53x vs rapidcsv) were measured with csv-parser's default speculative parallel parsing active (12 workers by inference from code defaults and timings) against single-threaded baselines.
status_note: Very actively developed by a single maintainer (v5.4.0 September 2026, last commit 2026-10-06, 1 open issue), MIT-licensed and easy to vendor as one header, but the 5.x speculative parser is only five months old and the published benchmark JSON (2026-05-08) predates releases 5.1-5.4.
